current.title: Highest Recorded Temperature
current.prompt: Rank the US states by highest temperature ever officially recorded within their borders.
current.disclaimer: Highest all-time official temperature per NOAA's State Climate Extremes Committee. Death Valley's 134°F (1913) remains debated but is the accepted official record. Includes Washington DC.
current.trivia: Death Valley's 134°F record from 1913 is the highest ever reliably recorded on Earth, though some meteorologists dispute it in favor of a 130°F reading from the same site in 2020.

findings.detail: Disclaimer states Death Valley's 134 F 'remains debated but is the accepted official record'. NOAA SCEC does still list CA 134 F, so 'accepted official record' is defensible, but calling it 'debated' without noting who disputes it (Christopher Burt et al.) may mislead. Minor.

current.title: Largest States by Total Area
current.prompt: Rank the US states by total area (land + water) in square miles.
current.disclaimer: Total area includes inland waters, coastal waters (within state jurisdiction), Great Lakes waters, and territorial waters — which is why Michigan (with huge Great Lakes waters) ranks higher on total than on land-only. Includes Washington DC.
current.trivia: Alaska is more than twice the area of Texas.

findings.detail: Disclaimer explicitly discusses Michigan's Great Lakes waters. Michigan is rank 11 in Q15 (not top-5), so this is not a hard leak; but pairing this question with Q16 ('Land Area'), where the disclaimer again spotlights Michigan, telegraphs MI's presence/absence to players who see both questions. Minor.

current.title: Longest River Wholly Within Borders
current.prompt: Name the US states with the longest single river that flows entirely within their own borders.
current.disclaimer: Longest single named river whose entire course lies within one state's boundaries. Rivers that cross state lines are excluded. Includes Washington DC.
current.trivia: Alaska's Kuskokwim River flows 702 miles from the Kuskokwim Mountains to the Bering Sea, all within Alaska, making it the longest single-state river in the U.S.

findings.detail: Prompt asks for 'longest single river that flows entirely within their own borders' but many answers reference an 'in-state segment' (e.g., OK Cimarron, VA James, IA Des Moines, MN St. Croix, AR Ouachita, NY Susquehanna, MS Pearl, MT Bighorn, CA San Joaquin, SD/ND/NM/AZ/NV/WY in-state segments, MA/CT Housatonic, NH Merrimack). These rivers cross state lines — contradicting the 'wholly within borders' prompt/disclaimer. Question definition contradicts data.

current.title: Most Colleges in a Single City
current.prompt: Rank the US states by the number of degree-granting colleges/universities in their most college-dense city.
current.disclaimer: Counts Title IV degree-granting institutions in a single principal city (not the whole metro). Boston's total is inflated by many small specialty and religious institutions. Includes Washington DC.
current.trivia: Greater Boston hosts more than 50 colleges, and Boston's Fenway/Longwood corridor alone has more medical schools than most US states.

findings.detail: All values expressed as 'N+ colleges' (open-ended buckets), which makes true ranking non-verifiable — e.g., '10+' at rank 12 (MD Baltimore) and rank 13 (FL Miami) could differ by many actual institutions but appear equal. Disclaimer acknowledges Boston is inflated but doesn't reconcile the plus-notation ordering.

current.title: Most Named Canyons
current.prompt: Name the US states with the most named canyons catalogued in the USGS Geographic Names Information System.
current.disclaimer: Counts of GNIS features whose names include 'Canyon' by state. Reflects naming convention as much as underlying topography. DC not included (source omits it).
current.trivia: Utah's dry climate and thick sedimentary rock layers make it the canyon-country capital of the U.S., with more named canyons than any other state.

findings.detail: Source cites 'USGS GNIS feature class Valley filtered to canyon names', but GNIS uses feature class 'Valley' as the parent class for canyons/gulches/ravines/hollows — filtering by name substring 'Canyon' inside 'Valley' is one valid approach, but the disclaimer note ('Reflects naming convention as much as underlying topography') is fine. Minor: rank 42 (VT) & 41 (NH) both '2 canyons' with no tie marker.

current.title: Most Named Peaks Over 5,000 ft
current.prompt: Name the US states with the most named summits above 5,000 feet in elevation.
current.disclaimer: Named summits above 5,000 ft (1,524 m) with recognized names in Peakbagger's state databases. Elevation cutoff is fixed, not prominence-adjusted. DC not included (source omits it).
current.trivia: Colorado's 5,000-ft threshold catches essentially every named peak in the state — its lowest point (the Arikaree River) sits at 3,317 ft.

findings.detail: CO=5,281 peaks is identical to CO=5,281 summits reported in the sibling 'Most Named Mountain Peaks' question (all GNIS summits regardless of elevation). It's implausible that 100% of Colorado's GNIS-named summits are above 5,000 ft — value appears copied from the other question rather than filtered by elevation.

current.title: Most National Parks
current.prompt: Rank the US states by number of designated National Parks (NPS 'National Park' designation only — not the 400+ broader NPS units).
current.disclaimer: 'National Park' is a specific NPS designation — the broader 'National Park System' includes 400+ units (monuments, seashores, historic sites) but the traditional 'National Park' title is much rarer. Excludes national monuments, historic sites, seashores, and recreation areas. DC not included (source omits it).
current.trivia: California leads with 9 parks, followed by Alaska with 8. Utah's 'Mighty 5' (Arches, Bryce, Canyonlands, Capitol Reef, Zion) all sit within a few hours' drive of each other.

answers.value: 1 National Park (Great Smoky, tied w/ NC)
1 National Park (Great Smoky, tied w/ TN) (tied)

findings.detail: Rank 13 and rank 16 both bucket states with '1 National Park' — TN, NC, OR at rank 13 but NM, NV, ND, AR, KY, OH, MI, MN, ME, VA, WV, SC, IN, MO at rank 16. All have the same count (1). Either all should be tied at rank 13 (jumping to rank 16 for next distinct value), or none should be. Also TN/NC share Great Smoky (single park spanning two states) — the 'tied w/ NC'/'tied w/ TN' annotation is inconsistent with treating each state as having 1 park independently.

current.title: Most Sunshine Hours Per Year
current.prompt: Rank the US states by average annual sunshine hours (statewide average).
current.disclaimer: Statewide averages derived from NOAA/NWS first-order station normals. Some states are averaged across multiple reporting stations. Includes Washington DC.
current.trivia: Yuma, Arizona records sun during roughly 90% of daylight hours annually — the sunniest place in the contiguous United States.

findings.detail: Values look like single-station highs (e.g. Yuma AZ) rather than statewide averages as claimed. AZ 3,806 hrs/yr matches Yuma specifically; statewide AZ average is far lower. HI at 2,835 is also too low for a headline sunshine metric if truly statewide. Prompt/disclaimer says 'statewide average', but figures appear to be first-order station bests, not state means.

current.title: States Crossed by the Continental Divide
current.prompt: Name the US states through which the Great (Continental) Divide of the Americas runs.
current.disclaimer: The Continental Divide separates Pacific-draining watersheds from Atlantic/Gulf-draining watersheds. In the US, it runs through five contiguous states plus Alaska. DC not included (topic is state-scoped).
current.trivia: The divide enters the US at Glacier National Park and exits at the New Mexico–Mexico border; it also crosses Alaska via the Brooks Range.

findings.detail: AK listed as on the Continental Divide of the Americas (Brooks Range). The Continental Divide of the Americas as commonly defined ends at Cape Prince of Wales area; the Brooks Range hosts the Arctic Divide, not the Continental Divide of the Americas. Disclaimer even acknowledges 'five contiguous states plus Alaska' — inconsistent framing.
